rewrites.summary:
A gubernatorial executive order (August 30, 2023) narrows the legal definitions of 'male' and 'female', declares a person's biological sex fixed at birth, ends state recognition of transgender people, and backs single-sex spaces for bathrooms and changing rooms - mostly resident-facing, but it signals an administration willing to use state machinery against gender identity.

The consequence axis is documented: the state houses trans prisoners by assigned birth sex in men's facilities — a transgender woman held in state custody (August 2022 federal ruling) was celled with a male sex offender who sexually assaulted her, and the court dismissed her failure-to-treat, surgery-denial and failure-to-protect claims, finding no deliberate indifference and no more than minimal injuries — so a trans woman in Nebraska custody faces birth-sex men's-prison placement with no proven judicial remedy against a violent cellmate.

Below the national score 0.36.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Legal observers recorded that opponents questioned the order's scope and legality when it was signed.

Federal framework turbulence: national Bureau of Prisons guidelines allowed trans prisoners to be transferred to facilities matching their gender identity (January 2017) until they were rescinded on May 11, 2018, returning placement to sex assigned at birth — so the state's birth-sex practice matches the national guideline in force since 2018.

The August 2022 ruling is the state's only documented trans-prisoner case: a federal district judge dismissed claims of failure to treat gender dysphoria, denial of gender-conforming surgery and failure to protect after the inmate was celled with a convicted sex offender who victimized her, writing that without medical evidence no reasonable jury could find deliberate indifference.
rewrites.localsOnly:
The executive order's direct bite is on state legal recognition - birth records, marker documentation and how state systems read a trans person's legal sex - which is resident-facing; what a visitor feels is the signal that state machinery is aimed at gender identity.

The order establishes the Women's Bill of Rights and directs state agencies to apply 'biological' definitions of sex, female, male, woman, girl, man, boy, mother and father.

Resident inmates: the documented state-custody practice is denial of gender-affirming care and gender-confirming surgery to a trans prisoner held in the men's prison, with the courts upholding the officials' conduct — a treatment and placement record a visitor meets only through arrest and detention.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
The national news report behind the claim that state recognition has ended was unreachable (403) at fetch time, so that characterization rests on the dossier note; the 0.36 benchmark has no surviving source in this record's list.

Prison axis: no Nebraska statute, regulation or department policy on trans-prisoner housing (birth-sex vs identity placement, special units, solitary) is documented — the placement practice rests on the 2022 lawsuit record alone, and the Bureau of Prisons guidance governs federal, not state, prisons.
rewrites.notes: rw001 VIS: folded 2 verified prison-axis sources (birth-sex men's-prison placement; August 2022 federal ruling) into visible fields as consequence-axis evidence; existing claims preserved verbatim; no external research.

rewrites.summary:
South Carolina's facility ban, enacted 2024, was expanded in 2026 to colleges and universities when the governor signed House Bill 4756 on May 15, 2026, requiring students in public schools, colleges and universities to use restrooms matching sex assigned at birth.

The consequence axis reaches custody: per a July 2026 monitoring tracker recorded in Metro Weekly's reporting, South Carolina is one of four states whose 'freeze-frame' policies restrict the treatments transgender inmates may receive while incarcerated — so a trans person imprisoned here faces restricted gender-affirming care — while no South Carolina case, ruling, special unit or segregation practice on where trans prisoners are housed is documented at all.

The July 2026 assessment counts the expansion, raising the state's tier to 'Worst Laws Passed'; South Carolina is part of the 18-state birth-sex-definition group and scores below the national score 0.36.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
The July 2026 assessment's national frame is 'Worst Policies In Effect', and its rubric ranks states by reading the adult and youth law text.

The only South Carolina trans-prisoner finding is second-hand: Metro Weekly's July 2026 report on Missouri's ban on gender-affirming care for inmates cites the Transitics tracker naming South Carolina (with Tennessee, Arkansas and Utah) among the freeze-frame states — a treatment restriction, not a housing-placement rule.
rewrites.localsOnly:
House Bill 4756 governs students across K-12 and higher education; the Senate amended the bill before passage, and the state's civil-liberties chapter framed it as discrimination against trans students.

The freeze-frame restriction governs residents held in state custody, limiting gender-affirming treatment a free resident could otherwise seek; it reaches a visitor only through arrest and detention.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
The dossier's 'Worst Laws Passed' tier label sits uneasily beside the assessment's own wording that the state is 'among the escalating states rather than the harshest tier'.

The 18-state grouping defining sex by birth is asserted in the current text, but no surviving source in this record's list supports it.

Prison axis: the freeze-frame status rests on a tracker cited in another state's news story, it describes treatment rather than placement, and no South Carolina rule, case, special unit or solitary/segregation practice for trans prisoners is documented — an unknown that cannot be read as a midpoint in a state whose facilities law assigns spaces by sex at birth.
rewrites.notes: rw001 VIS: folded verified prison-axis source (freeze-frame treatment restriction via Metro Weekly/Transitics; no placement rule, case, special unit or segregation practice documented) into visible fields; no external research.

rewrites.summary:
Tennessee is the only state in the country with a standing criminal ban on gender-expressive performance: the Adult Entertainment Act (2023) criminalises 'adult cabaret entertainment' — defined to include 'male or female impersonators' — anywhere a child could see it, at up to 11 months 29 days and a $2,500 fine for a first offence and a 1–6 year felony on repeat. The ban is enforceable and current: the appeals court revived it on standing grounds and the Supreme Court declined review (February 2025), so a visitor presenting in drag faces live charging exposure today rather than a dead-letter law.

The consequence axis reaches custody: under the Riley Gaines Women's Safety and Protection Act (2026) transgender inmates are to be placed in prisons based on sex assigned at birth, and since April 2024 state law has banned gender-affirming care for Tennessee inmates — so a trans visitor arrested here is housed by birth sex with no gender-affirming care allowed behind the walls.

For practical safety, killings of trans women run at 7.8 per 100k per year — above the general national homicide rate.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Adjacent litigation and policy flux: the Supreme Court upheld the state's ban on gender-affirming care for minors in June 2025, and the drag ban's constitutionality has never been decided on the merits. A civil-liberties suit over a district attorney's threat to charge a 2023 Pride event also remains ongoing.

The Riley Gaines Act's adjacent provision also bars trans women from women's shelters — a facility restriction beyond prisons attached to the same 2026 statute.
rewrites.localsOnly:
Since 2026 the state has also mandated birth-sex placement in prisons and shelters — a resident-facing facility practice.

The April 2024 in-prison ban on gender-affirming care governs the treatment of residents held in state custody.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
No drag-ban prosecutions are publicly reported, so actual charging practice is unverified. The killing-rate figure rests on 10 recorded deaths (2008–2025), treated as an undercount floor.

Prison axis: the birth-sex placement mandate is statutory (2026), but no Tennessee case, ruling, special unit or solitary/segregation practice for trans prisoners is documented; the prison and shelter provisions come from a single Wikipedia state-rights article, the only prison-axis source in this record.
rewrites.notes: rw001 VIS: folded prison-axis facts (2026 Riley Gaines birth-sex placement mandate; April 2024 in-prison gender-affirming-care ban) into visible fields; no external research.

rewrites.summary:
Texas operates one of the country's most actively enforced anti-trans regimes. Its facilities law (the SB 8 'Women's Privacy Act', in force 4 December 2025) produced enforcement within days: state troopers checked identification at women's restrooms in the Capitol while cities and campuses adopted sharply divergent compliance and evasion policies, and the attorney general opened the first state bathroom-law enforcement inquiry of its kind — against an Austin school district, escalated with a second records demand in April 2026 after a tip-line complaint.

The consequence axis reaches custody on two fronts: the Women's Privacy Act expressly applies to prisons and other state government buildings — but on restroom use matching the sex on one's birth certificate, not on cell or facility assignment — while in Gibson v. Collier (2019) the Texas prison system denied a transgender inmate gender-confirmation surgery under its official policy, and the courts affirmed no deliberate indifference, treating the refusal as a permissible medical choice, leaving a trans person in Texas custody without a proven judicial remedy for denial of gender-affirming care.

Violence exposure is the national worst in absolute terms: 44 recorded killings of trans women over 2008–2025 (about 7.6 per 100k trans women per year; the monitoring project frames all rates as undercount floors). A July 2026 law-by-law legal-risk assessment grades Texas in its top 'Do Not Travel' tier.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
LGB-facing visibility is rolling back too: Arlington's city council rescinded its LGBTQ non-discrimination ordinance (Dec 2025) and Arlington Pride suspended its 2026 events; a Houston-area venue pulled out of Katy Pride under school-board pressure.

Litigation flux: in Gibson v. Collier (2019) a federal court denied the state's immunity defences but ruled against the transgender inmate on the Eighth Amendment claim, and the Fifth Circuit affirmed the dismissal (with a dissenting opinion on summary-judgement procedure) — documentation of Texas' denial practice more than a change in it.
rewrites.localsOnly:
Document governance is resident-facing but nationally anomalous: DPS has ignored court-ordered gender-marker changes and built a database of applicants seeking them.

The denial practice is resident-facing: Vanessa Lynn Gibson, a transgender woman incarcerated with the Texas Department of Criminal Justice and diagnosed with gender dysphoria, was denied gender-confirmation surgery because the department's official treatment policy excluded it.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Prison axis: the Women's Privacy Act's prison reach is restroom-use only — no Texas statute, rule, case or ruling on cell or facility assignment for trans prisoners (birth-sex vs identity, special units, solitary/segregation) is documented; Gibson v. Collier is a treatment case, not a placement ruling.
rewrites.notes: rw001 VIS: folded prison-axis facts (Women's Privacy Act restroom reach into prisons; Gibson v. Collier treatment denial) into visible fields; no external research.

rewrites.summary:
Afghanistan under the Taliban — the nation's current ruling movement — is the most hostile environment on this map for a transgender person. A 2024 Morality Law obliges the regime's virtue police to prevent "homosexuality" and "lesbianism", including "even if with one's own spouse"; the ruling movement applies the death penalty for same-sex relations under its interpretation of Sharia; and documented practice against LGBTIQ people includes beatings, sexual violence in detention, forced confessions, and house-to-house searches. Transgender residents report living in hiding, in windowless rooms, for years.

There is no legal recognition, no protection, no functioning consular protection, and no tourism infrastructure that would allow a visitor to blend in. A discovered trans visitor would face the same enforcement apparatus as local LGBTIQ people: detention with routine sexual and physical abuse of queer detainees, prosecution for moral crimes, and corporal punishment that international experts say is escalating into 2026. The prison-housing axis is thin but must not read as neutral: nothing is documented on where trans prisoners are held — no birth-sex vs identity housing rule, no trans special units, no solitary or segregation practice — while Human Rights Watch / OutRight International (January 2022, 60 interviews) documents wrongful-detention risk, threats, assault and blackmail of LGBTI people since the takeover; in a criminalising regime with no recourse, an undocumented placement practice means a detained trans visitor is held at the regime's discretion amid the documented abuse of queer detainees, not under any protected standard.

This is the reference point for the very bottom of the risk scale.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
The applicable legal regime is layered and shifting: penal-code "sodomy" provisions carry up to two years, while a Sharia-reference clause permits the death penalty for same-sex activity and the 2024 Morality Law added surveillance duties; flogging documented by international experts nearly doubled in 2025 to at least 1,110 people.

Asylum-framework context: international guidance treats LGBTIQ people in the country as those perceived to transgress religious and social norms, and refugee-led organisations abroad document systematic persecution — context for the regime's treatment, not visitor-facing advice.

Enforcement context: the Human Rights Watch / OutRight International report (26 January 2022) records Taliban members using leaked personal data to pursue individuals considered gay or gender-nonconforming, and it calls on the regime to end discrimination and violence against LGBTI people.
rewrites.localsOnly:
Resident-facing documentation: trans and gay residents report living in hiding, in windowless rooms, for years; family, neighbour and partner abuse surged after the 2021 takeover; security officials pursue gay men and trans women more systematically than in earlier rule.

Interview-based reports from residents in-country and abroad record physical and sexual assault, arbitrary detention and public flogging for alleged same-sex relations, with visibly transgender people facing the gravest risks including exploitation and violence.

Human Rights Watch / OutRight International's 26 January 2022 report (43 pages, 60 interviews with residents in-country and abroad) is the specific source base for those accounts of threats, assault, blackmail and wrongful-detention risk after the 15 August 2021 takeover; it describes no trans-prisoner placement practice at all.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
Armed conflict, terrorism, kidnapping, and the arbitrary detention of foreign nationals for leverage are severe risks for every visitor to Afghanistan, independent of any personal characteristic.

Unresolved or unverifiable: enforcement figures rest on 2022-23 interview-based reports and 2025-26 international flogging counts rather than the regime's own statistics; most accounts predate the 2024 Morality Law's implementation, so current on-the-ground practice is inferred rather than directly documented; no tourist entry pathway exists to test in practice.

Prison-housing axis: there is no evidence at all on birth-sex vs identity placement, trans special units, or solitary/segregation practice — the only prison-relevant finding is general wrongful-detention danger; that gap is treated as danger here, because a regime that criminalises same-sex conduct and abuses queer detainees cannot be assumed to place trans prisoners safely.
rewrites.notes: rw001 VIS: folded HRW/OutRight prison-axis finding (detention danger documented; no placement practice) into visible fields with thin-data extrapolation per LANE_SPECS rule 8b; no external research.
